statement: For any finite or infinite sequence x_1, x_2, ... in a Euclidean space V there is a corresponding sequence y_1, y_2, ... in V such that for every k: (a) y_k is orthogonal to every element of L(y_1, ..., y_{k-1}); (b) L(y_1, ..., y_k) = L(x_1, ..., x_k); and (c) the sequence is unique except for scalar factors. Its proof is constructive and by induction, taking y_1 = x_1 and subtracting suitable multiples of the earlier y_i from x_{r+1}.

anchors.quote: THEOREM 15.13. ORTHOGONALIZATION THEOREM. Let $x_1, x_2, \ldots,$ be a finite or infinite sequence of elements in a Euclidean space $V$ ,
(a) The element $y_{k}$ is orthogonal to every element in the subspace $L(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{k - 1})$ .
(b) The subspace spanned by $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{k}$ is the same as that spanned by $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}$ :

statement: The explicit construction y_1 = x_1 and y_{r+1} = x_{r+1} - sum_{i=1}^{r} ((x_{r+1}, y_i)/(y_i, y_i)) y_i (formula 15.15), which turns an independent set x_1, ..., x_k in a Euclidean space into an orthogonal set of nonzero elements y_1, ..., y_k spanning the same subspace. Each step subtracts from x_{r+1} its projection along every earlier y_i.

anchors.quote: The construction is called the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process, in honor of J. P. Gram
These formulas describe the Gram-Schmidt process for constructing an orthogonal set of nonzero elements $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{k}$ which spans the same subspace as a given independent set
In the Gram-Schmidt process (15.15), we construct the element $y_{r+1}$ by subtracting from $x_{r+1}$ the projection of $x_{r+1}$ along each of the earlier elements $y_{1},\ldots,y_{r}$ .

name_en: Uniqueness of the orthogonalized sequence up to scalar factors
name_zh: 正交化序列在相差标量因子下的唯一性
statement: Part (c) of the orthogonalization theorem: if y_1', y_2', ... is another sequence in V satisfying properties (a) and (b), then for each k there is a scalar c_k with y_k' = c_k y_k. The proof writes y_{r+1}' = z_r + c_{r+1} y_{r+1} with z_r in L(y_1, ..., y_r) and shows z_r is orthogonal to itself, hence z_r = O.

anchors.quote: (c) The sequence $y_1, y_2, \ldots$ , is unique, except for scalar factors.
if $y_1', y_2', \ldots$ , is another sequence of elements in $V$ satisfying properties (a) and (b), then for each $k$ there is a scalar $c_k$ such that $y_k' = c_k y_k$ .

statement: A basis of a Euclidean space whose elements form an orthogonal set of nonzero elements. Applying the Gram-Schmidt process to a basis x_1, ..., x_k of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space produces an orthogonal basis y_1, ..., y_k of that same space, so every finite-dimensional Euclidean space has one.

anchors.quote: Every finite-dimensional linear space has a finite basis. If the space is Euclidean, we can always construct an orthogonal basis.
if $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}$ is a basis for a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, then $y_{1}, \ldots, y_{k}$ is an orthogonal basis for the same space.
The set $\{y_{1}, y_{2}\}$ is an orthogonal basis for this subspace.

name_en: Every finite-dimensional Euclidean space has an orthonormal basis (Theorem 15.14)
name_zh: 每个有限维欧几里得空间都有正交规范基(定理 15.14)
statement: Theorem 15.14 states that every finite-dimensional Euclidean space has an orthonormal basis. It is obtained as a corollary of Theorem 15.13: orthogonalize a finite basis by the Gram-Schmidt process, then normalize each resulting element.
